It has been a constant, steady state of worry, and I haven't really had any periods where I felt better or got a break from it.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned losing enjoyment in activities like hiking and painting, but can you tell me if there are any activities or situations where you still feel some pleasure or interest, even if it's fleeting?\n\nPatient: To be honest, it is currently very difficult to find enjoyment or interest in anything at all. My brain just feels stuck in high gear, constantly looping through \"what-if\" scenarios about the practice and my retirement, rather than feeling depressed.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how long you've been experiencing this intense worry and loss of enjoyment in activities, and has it been a constant state or have you had periods where you felt better in between?\n\nPatient: This has been going on pretty steadily for about a year and a quarter, ever since I really started trying to line up my retirement and the buy-in with the younger dentists. It has been a constant, steady state of worry, and I haven't really had any periods where I felt better or got a break from it.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned losing enjoyment in activities like hiking and painting, but can you tell me if there are any activities or situations where you still feel some pleasure or interest, even if it's fleeting?\n\nPatient: To be honest, it is currently very difficult to find enjoyment or interest in anything at all. Even when I attempt to do something else, the constant worry and racing thoughts about the practice block out any fleeting sense of pleasure. It just leaves me feeling completely drained instead.\n\nDoctor: Are there any small, everyday things that still bring you some sense of pleasure or satisfaction, even if it's minor, like a good cup of coffee or a beautiful sunset?\n\nPatient: To be honest, even those small moments don't bring much satisfaction anymore. Things like having a cup of coffee or walking the dog just feel like a chore because my mind is constantly running numbers about the practice. I'm just too drained to appreciate them.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling anxious and worried, but not necessarily sad or empty, can you tell me if you've had any days in the past two weeks where you didn't feel anxious or worried at all, or has it been a constant presence?\n\nPatient: No, there hasn't been a single day in the past two weeks where I haven't felt anxious. My mind feels constantly stuck in high gear, looping through thoughts about the practice day and night, and I haven't had a single day where I felt truly relaxed or free from this worry.\n\nDoctor: You've described feeling anxious and worried, but also mentioned losing interest in activities and feeling drained; can you tell me if you've had any thoughts about death or wishing you weren't alive, or are your thoughts more focused on the worries about your practice and future?\n\nPatient: No, I definitely don't have any thoughts of death or wishing I wasn't alive. My mind is just entirely consumed by the constant, looping worries about the practice, my employees' security, the associates' buy-in, and my retirement future. I just want to find a way to quiet my mind.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities or things that you used to enjoy that you still find yourself looking forward to, even if you don't end up feeling pleasure from them when you do them?\n\nPatient: I still think about wanting to paint, go hiking, or socialize, and I really wish I could. But when it comes to actually setting up my painting gear or getting out on a trail, the sheer effort of starting feels completely overwhelming. I'm just too exhausted and mentally preoccupied to actually do them or find any enjoyment.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling anxious and worried, but also losing interest in activities; can you tell me if you think your lack of interest in activities is more due to your anxiety and worry, or if you feel like you're just not interested in things anymore, even if your anxiety were to decrease?\n\nPatient: It is definitely because of the anxiety and worry. My mind is so constantly consumed by the practice and I feel too physically and mentally drained to even try. If I could just stop this constant worrying and get my energy back, I would gladly return to painting and hiking.\n\nDoctor: If your anxiety and worries about the practice were to significantly decrease, do you think you would regain your interest and pleasure in activities like painting and hiking, or do you think you would still struggle with feeling empty or disconnected from things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: I absolutely believe I would regain my interest once this constant worry and mental exhaustion are resolved. I didn't stop because I lost my love for painting and hiking, but because my mind is constantly looping over the practice and I feel too physically and mentally drained to even set up my easel or go for a walk.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely resolve your worries about the practice and your retirement, do you think you would still feel a lack of interest or pleasure in activities, or would that improve as well?\n\nPatient: I believe it would definitely improve. My lack of interest in painting or hiking is entirely tied to this constant worrying and physical exhaustion. If my mind could finally quiet down, I'm confident I would have the energy and mental presence to enjoy those activities again.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your main issue is anxiety and worry, but you've also experienced a loss of interest in activities; can you tell me if you think you would still feel anxious and worried if you were able to regain your interest and pleasure in activities like painting and hiking?\n\nPatient: Yes, I would definitely still feel anxious, because the worry is the root cause preventing me from enjoying those hobbies in the first place. Even if I forced myself to go hiking or paint, my mind would just keep looping and branching off with thoughts about the practice, making it impossible to distract myself. The anxiety would remain because I simply cannot shut off these racing thoughts, even during activities I used to love.\n\nDoctor: You've described both anxiety and a loss of interest in activities, but can you tell me if you've experienced any significant changes in your appetite or sleep patterns since your worrying started?\n\nPatient: My appetite hasn't really changed, but my sleep has been absolutely terrible. Most nights I lie awake for an hour or two running numbers about the practice in my head, and even when I do fall asleep, I wake up at three or four in the morning worrying about payroll or the associates and just can't drift back off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt consistently sad, empty, or depressed, separate from your current anxiety and worry about the practice?\n\nPatient: No, I've never really experienced periods of feeling consistently sad, empty, or depressed like that. My struggle has always been this constant, overwhelming worry and anxiety about the practice rather than feeling down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical day and how your anxiety and worry affect your daily functioning and relationships, and are there any times when your worry seems to peak or worsen?\n\nPatient: During the day, it's causing me to make small charting mistakes at the office and lose concentration during procedures, while at home, my wife says I'm barely present and I've been turning down social plans because I'm so drained. The worry definitely peaks at night, where I'll lie awake for hours running numbers or wake up at 3:00 AM unable to get back to sleep. It's incredibly frustrating because I just can't seem to turn it off.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your lack of interest in activities is a direct result of your anxiety and worry, or do you feel like you've lost interest in things independently of your anxiety?\n\nPatient: It is absolutely a direct result of my anxiety and worry. I haven't lost interest in hiking, painting, or socializing on my own, but my mind is constantly spinning with worries about the practice, leaving me too keyed up and drained to participate. The constant worrying just leaves me with absolutely no mental or physical energy to engage in or enjoy those things.\n\nDoctor: If you were to wake up tomorrow and all your worries about the practice were suddenly and completely resolved, do you think you would still feel a general sense of sadness or emptiness, or would you primarily feel relieved and able to enjoy activities again?"

It has been a constant, steady state of worry, and I haven't really had any periods where I felt better or got a break from it.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned losing enjoyment in activities like hiking and painting, but can you tell me if there are any activities or situations where you still feel some pleasure or interest, even if it's fleeting?\n\nPatient: To be honest, it is currently very difficult to find enjoyment or interest in anything at all. Even when I attempt to do something else, the constant worry and racing thoughts about the practice block out any fleeting sense of pleasure. It just leaves me feeling completely drained instead.\n\nDoctor: Are there any small, everyday things that still bring you some sense of pleasure or satisfaction, even if it's minor, like a good cup of coffee or a beautiful sunset?\n\nPatient: To be honest, even those small moments don't bring much satisfaction anymore. I'm just too drained to appreciate them.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling anxious and worried, but not necessarily sad or empty, can you tell me if you've had any days in the past two weeks where you didn't feel anxious or worried at all, or has it been a constant presence?\n\nPatient: No, there hasn't been a single day in the past two weeks where I haven't felt anxious. But when it comes to actually setting up my painting gear or getting out on a trail, the sheer effort of starting feels completely overwhelming. I'm just too exhausted and mentally preoccupied to actually do them or find any enjoyment.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling anxious and worried, but also losing interest in activities; can you tell me if you think your lack of interest in activities is more due to your anxiety and worry, or if you feel like you're just not interested in things anymore, even if your anxiety were to decrease?\n\nPatient: It is definitely because of the anxiety and worry. My mind is so constantly consumed by the practice and I feel too physically and mentally drained to even try. If I could just stop this constant worrying and get my energy back, I would gladly return to painting and hiking.\n\nDoctor: If your anxiety and worries about the practice were to significantly decrease, do you think you would regain your interest and pleasure in activities like painting and hiking, or do you think you would still struggle with feeling empty or disconnected from things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: I absolutely believe I would regain my interest once this constant worry and mental exhaustion are resolved. I didn't stop because I lost my love for painting and hiking, but because my mind is constantly looping over the practice and I feel too physically and mentally drained to even set up my easel or go for a walk.\n\nDoctor: If you were able to completely resolve your worries about the practice and your retirement, do you think you would still feel a lack of interest or pleasure in activities, or would that improve as well?\n\nPatient: I believe it would definitely improve. Even if I forced myself to go hiking or paint, my mind would just keep looping and branching off with thoughts about the practice, making it impossible to distract myself. The anxiety would remain because I simply cannot shut off these racing thoughts, even during activities I used to love.\n\nDoctor: You've described both anxiety and a loss of interest in activities, but can you tell me if you've experienced any significant changes in your appetite or sleep patterns since your worrying started?\n\nPatient: My appetite hasn't really changed, but my sleep has been absolutely terrible. Most nights I lie awake for an hour or two running numbers about the practice in my head, and even when I do fall asleep, I wake up at three or four in the morning worrying about payroll or the associates and just can't drift back off.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks where you felt consistently sad, empty, or depressed, separate from your current anxiety and worry about the practice?\n\nPatient: No, I've never really experienced periods of feeling consistently sad, empty, or depressed like that. My struggle has always been this constant, overwhelming worry and anxiety about the practice rather than feeling down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a typical day and how your anxiety and worry affect your daily functioning and relationships, and are there any times when your worry seems to peak or worsen?\n\nPatient: During the day, it's causing me to make small charting mistakes at the office and lose concentration during procedures, while at home, my wife says I'm barely present and I've been turning down social plans because I'm so drained. It's just this non-stop loop of anxiety about the practice that is completely exhausting me, and if that were gone, I know I'd finally have the energy to relax at home and enjoy painting and hiking again.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel like you're worrying about your worry itself, or if your worry is always focused on specific issues like the practice and retirement?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really worry about the worry itself; my thoughts are always focused on those concrete issues like the future of my practice, the associates' buy-in, and my staff's security. My loss of interest in painting, hiking, and socializing stems directly from being completely drained by the constant worry—it honestly feels like someone pulled the plug on my batteries. It's just this non-stop loop of anxiety about the practice that is completely exhausting me, and if that were gone, I know I'd finally have the energy to relax at home and enjoy painting and hiking again.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel like you're worrying about your worry itself, or if your worry is always focused on specific issues like the practice and retirement?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really worry about the worry itself; my thoughts are always focused on those concrete issues like the future of my practice, the associates' buy-in, and my staff's security. Even if I forced myself to go hiking or paint, my mind would just keep looping and branching off with thoughts about the practice, making it impossible to distract myself.
